source: Pitt (2001) The dilemma of case studies: toward a Heraclitian philosophy of science
finding: Two-horned dilemma. If a case is picked because it fits a philosophical point, the data may be bent to fit. If one starts from a case, one cannot generalise from one, two or three cases.
numbers: No numbers. Abstract seen via repository page; quoted in Scholl 2018.
quote: if the case is selected because it exemplifies the philosophical point, then it is not clear that the historical data hasn't been manipulated
limits: Full text not read; position taken from Burian, Scholl and Herfeld who quote it.
agent_relevance: Names two failure modes our agent must guard against when it uses a past case as proof: choosing the case after the claim (selection) and generalising from a handful (small n).

source: Burian (2001) The dilemma of case studies resolved
finding: Burian restates Pitt: top-down testing makes sampling and interpretation biased; bottom-up gives hasty generalisation, since even a few hundred cases cannot represent diverse science. He says the dilemma is ill-founded because science has local consensus and cases can be grouped.
numbers: No statistics. Claim: 'even a few hundred case studies' are not enough to generalise. Names Agassi, Feyerabend, Kuhn, Lakatos, Laudan as holding similar views.
quote: A series of case studies--even a few hundred case studies--does not provide a sufficient basis for generalising about science
limits: Position paper by a biologist-philosopher; claims rest on his own cases (Brachet, Jacob and Monod), not on a test of the method.
agent_relevance: Rule: a pile of cases is not a sample. Treat cases as sources of mechanisms and methods, not as votes.

source: Burian (2001) - Lakatos and Laudan escape routes
finding: Lakatos's escape: expose each methodology to all cases of all rivals, drop the trivial 'all science is rational', and prefer the one that rates the most cases as sound. Laudan's variant: use scientists' touchstone judgements. Burian says both assume credit and blame were assigned correctly, with no independent standpoint to check.
numbers: None. Lakatos 1971/1972; Laudan 1977.
quote: No independent standpoint is available to certify the correctness of this assumption
limits: Critique by Burian; Lakatos and Laudan might reply. Original texts not opened.
agent_relevance: Counting cases a rule 'explains' is circular if the rule decides which cases are good. A check must come from something the rule did not grade.

source: Burian (2001) - grouped case studies: longitudinal and comparative
finding: Burian says the powerful designs are grouped studies. Longitudinal studies follow a problem over time. Comparative studies compare labs, disciplines, places or tools on one problem. Context is limited by showing it was relevant to the work.
numbers: No numbers. Lists about a dozen of his own studies as examples.
limits: Method advice, untested; 'relevant context' is a judgement call.
agent_relevance: Store cases in groups (same problem, different settings or times) so the agent can see what changes with context rather than reading one case alone.

source: Burian (2001) - Brachet case: exploratory experimentation
finding: Brachet studied nucleic acids from 1927 with almost no guiding theory and found DNA only in the nucleus and most RNA in the cytoplasm, overturning the idea that RNA is plant and DNA animal nucleic acid. By 1952 he had a scheme close to later protein synthesis accounts. Burian says top-down philosophy misses this mode of work.
numbers: Dates: work from 1927; RNAse crystallised 1938; differential staining by 1940; scheme in 1952 book.
quote: No theoretical principle, guideline, or expectation about the distribution of the nucleic acids shaped Brachet's findings
limits: One case. Burian says exploratory experiment is common but gives no count.
agent_relevance: A good method claim can come from a case with no hypothesis-testing in it. The agent should allow an explore mode (collect, trace, triangulate) that is not graded as a failed hypothesis test.

source: Burian (2001) - Jacob and Monod and cross-discipline triangulation
finding: Most mid-century molecular biology was done in pairs from different disciplines (Beadle and Tatum, Luria and Delbruck, Watson and Crick, Jacob and Monod, Meselson and Stahl). Burian argues this gives several independent routes to a theoretical entity and corrects each discipline's built-in bias. Some Jacob-Monod experiments neither confirmed nor refuted the theory but opened new questions.
numbers: Six named pairs from Jacob (1998: 47).
limits: Anecdotal selection of six pairs; no base rate.
agent_relevance: Independent routes beat repeated draws. This matches G4: samples from one model are not independent; use different methods or tools for real independence.

source: Scholl (2018) Scenes from a marriage: the confrontation model of HPS
finding: The confrontation model treats HPS as an empirical science: philosophical accounts are tested against historical cases. Scholl argues its problems come from framing it as hypothetico-deductive testing or enumerative induction, and that an iterative concrete-to-abstract model removes most of them.
numbers: No statistics. Key refs: Giere 1973 and 1985; Hull 1992; Laudan et al. 1986 (Synthese 69: 141-223).
quote: the confrontation model's difficulties are artifactual
limits: Draft of 23 Jan 2018 (forthcoming J. Phil. of History). Normative argument; no empirical test of the proposal.
agent_relevance: Gives the agent a name and a rule for using cases: describe concretely, abstract, then check scope on further cases. Not 'prove by example'.

source: Laudan, Donovan, Laudan et al. (1986) Scientific change: philosophical models and historical research (VPI project), as described by Scholl
finding: The VPI project aimed to test post-positivist models of scientific change (Kuhn, Lakatos, Laudan) against history. Earlier tests were called perfunctory and superficial. Their two steps: split each model into separately testable claims, and operationalise each claim.
numbers: No numbers. Synthese 69(2): 141-223; book Scrutinizing Science (Donovan, Laudan, Laudan eds., 1988).
quote: Nothing resembling the standards of testing that these very authors insist upon within science
limits: Original not opened. Scholl notes no handbook on naturalistic theory testing was ever produced.
agent_relevance: Modularise a big method claim into small checkable claims and operationalise each before using any case as evidence. This fits how we should split schema rules into testable parts.

source: Giere (1973, 1985) HPS: intimate relationship or marriage of convenience; Philosophy of science naturalized, as described by Scholl
finding: In 1973 Giere found the case for tight history-philosophy links unmade: circularity (evidence needs a prior notion of evidence) and normativity (facts do not give norms). By 1985 he judged a priori foundations (Carnap, Reichenbach, Popper, Bayesianism) hopeless and said the study of science must be a science.
numbers: None.
quote: the study of science must itself be a science
limits: Second-hand via Scholl.
agent_relevance: Circularity worry applies to us: judging cases needs a notion of good method. Break it by using outcome checks (code runs, answer verifies), not the schema's own opinion.

source: Hull (1992, 1998) Testing philosophical claims about science, as described by Scholl
finding: Hull's two-by-two of views on empirical evidence in science versus in the study of science; he took the view that both need data. He proposed testing norms by getting scientists to adopt them and seeing whether they succeed more.
numbers: None.
quote: if those scientists who adopt your views are even more successful in attaining their epistemic goals, then possibly there is something to be said for these norms
limits: Second-hand via Scholl; the adoption test was proposed, not run here.
agent_relevance: This is the closest idea to an A/B test of a method rule. Our bench harness does exactly this for schema rules (arms with and without a rule).

source: Schickore (2011) More thoughts on HPS: another 20 years later, as described by Scholl
finding: Schickore lists four problems for the confrontation model: case-study generalisation (Pitt), theory-laden historical data, history may not give data philosophers need (Pfizer Award winners focus on images, non-scientists, commerce), and why use history rather than recent science. She prefers a hermeneutic picture: case judgments and concepts brought into equilibrium.
numbers: Basis: recent Pfizer Award winners of the History of Science Society; no counts given.
quote: Initial case judgments ... and provisional analytic concepts are gradually reconciled until they are brought into equilibrium
limits: Second-hand via Scholl and Herfeld.
agent_relevance: Case judgments and concepts adjust each other. The agent should be allowed to revise its concept after reading a case, but only with logged reasons.

source: Scholl (2018) - three-operation model of inquiry
finding: Borrowing from mechanism studies in biology: (1) study exemplars to describe concrete mechanisms, (2) articulate an abstract schema, (3) test its scope on more cases. The steps are iterative, not a sequence. Moving from concrete to abstract is not ampliative; only scope claims are counts of further instances.
numbers: Examples: squid giant axon for neural transmission; cow heart mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation; gene 'expression' redefined from Mendel/Morgan (traits) to Beadle/Tatum (enzymes) to Jacob/Monod (regulatory and structural proteins).
quote: Enumeration, yes: We study how many other cases fit a given abstract description. But no induction in the sense of ampliative inference
limits: A conceptual proposal; no data on how well it works in practice.
agent_relevance: A usable procedure: describe case, write abstract rule, list which further cases fit. State generality as 'known instances', not as a law.

source: Scholl (2018) - how the model answers Pitt's selection-bias horn
finding: On the three-operation model, concrete descriptions are used only to derive abstract descriptions and to find their scope. The model never advises inferring a thesis's generality from a few cases. Extrapolating between cases needs a reason they are related (shared teaching and imitation), and it only guides the next case.
numbers: None.
quote: The model never advises us to leverage individual concrete descriptions, or even a handful of them, in order to infer the generality of a philosophical thesis
limits: Spurious support is still easy if scope counts ignore unfavourable cases; the paper says extra warrant is needed.
agent_relevance: Rule for the agent: a case supports a scope statement only if cases were sought by a rule that also finds counter-cases; cross-case transfer needs a stated link.

source: Chang (2011) Beyond case-studies: history as philosophy; cyclical model, as described by Herfeld (2025)
finding: Chang replaces the representational, inductive link between a general concept and a case with a cycle. Concepts are needed to identify episodes, and episodes shape the concepts. Iteration refines abstract concepts, aimed at abstraction not generalisation.
numbers: None.
limits: Second-hand via Herfeld; Herfeld says Chang leaves open how to make the iteration systematic or how to select cases.
agent_relevance: Supports a loop, not a one-shot proof: case, concept, case. Matches our rule of revising only on real output.

source: Herfeld (2025) Enhancing the function of case studies: network analysis in integrated HPS
finding: Argues that network analysis can address case-selection bias and unwarranted generalisation in HPS by giving explicit, repeatable rules for data, network and analysis. It supports three case-study functions: concept generation, refinement, and empirical justification. It cannot replace traditional philosophical work.
numbers: Synthese 205:167, 25 pages. Received 28 Jan 2022, accepted 9 Oct 2024.
quote: network analysis ... cannot replace more traditional philosophical methods
limits: Programmatic. Shows the method by re-describing an earlier study (Herfeld and Doehne 2019), not by a new test.
agent_relevance: Selection rules written in advance, with thresholds, make case choice auditable. We can apply rule-based case retrieval for the agent.

source: Herfeld (2025) - the rational choice model-transfer example (Herfeld and Doehne 2019)
finding: Data rules: all Scopus items from 1984-2014 citing von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games (1944), then their cited items from 1944-1970. Edge rule: two works co-cited at least 3 times; drop an edge if the works are more than 5 years apart. Analysis: clusters = target domains; densest nodes = 'epistemic core'; one 'translator' per cluster. Output: four roles (innovator, elaborator, translator, specialist).
numbers: Thresholds: >=3 co-citations; <=5 years apart; periods 1944-1970 and 1984-2014.
limits: Co-citation is a proxy for transfer. Thresholds are justified by intuition, not tuned or validated. Herfeld lists limitations of the method.
agent_relevance: A concrete model of 'rules before cases': explicit thresholds and a fixed pipeline that could be applied to any new episode. Same style our case library needs.

source: Herfeld (2025) - Pitt's dilemma restated and the three functions of cases
finding: Cases serve three functions: generative (new facts and concepts), refinement (revise concepts), justification (empirical support for armchair claims). The 'confrontation model' (Schickore) supposes representative cases. Philosophers can keep confirming old beliefs and historians dislike oversimplified histories.
numbers: Cites Chang 2012, Kinzel 2015, Scholl and Raz 2016 for the three functions; Kinzel lists four.
limits: Functions are a classification, not measured.
agent_relevance: Label each use of a case: generate an idea, refine a rule, or justify a rule. Only the third is evidence, and it needs the strictest controls.

source: Kinzel (2015) Narrative and evidence: how can case studies from the history of science support claims in the philosophy of science?
finding: Kinzel argues about how historical narratives can work as evidence for philosophical claims; Herfeld says she names four functions of cases.
numbers: No numbers. Studies in HPS Part A 49: 48-57. Semantic Scholar lists 51 citations.
limits: Full text not accessible (publisher check page blocked); only the secondary description above.
agent_relevance: Mark as to-read. Narrative evidence is relevant because our agent's cases are short text records.

source: Lakatos (1971, 1972) all-cases test, as described by Burian
finding: Lakatos's proposal sets every methodology against all cases from all rivals, drops the trivial 'all science is rational', and prefers the one that rates the most cases as sound. Burian calls this impractical and circular.
numbers: None.
limits: Described by Burian; the Lakatos texts were not opened.
agent_relevance: A tally across cases is only valid if case verdicts come from a neutral judge.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: evaluating AI agents on the rediscovery of scientific insights
finding: Benchmark that uses published findings as cases: agents get only the research question, run experiments, and are scored on rediscovering documented claims. Strongest agent (Claude Code) averages F1 46.7. Failures are mostly in planning and in going from evidence to conclusion, especially control design.
numbers: 30 core LLM-behaviour tasks plus 10 cross-domain tasks; 3 runs per task; judge gpt-5.2; best per-task F1: Lost in the Middle 91.7, Persona with Catch 88.6, CoT Without Prompting 82.6 (Claude Code) vs 26.4 (OpenHands gpt-5). Human check on 33% of reference instances: precision 0.95, recall 0.86, F1 0.89.
limits: Mostly ML-behaviour papers; LLM judge for claim matching; high run-to-run variance; coarse contamination checks.
agent_relevance: Case replay as a test: use known results as ground truth to test the agent's method, and expect weakness in control design. Add an explicit baseline or control step.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench - error analysis
finding: False positive claims are mostly Contradictory or Unrelated (76.4% to 95.0% depending on agent); Alternative but reasonable conclusions are only 4.5% to 10.9%. In the racial-bias case every agent skipped the race-free baseline and injected labels into notes still carrying demographic cues; two agents scored 0.0 F1.
numbers: Example: OpenHands (gpt-5) false positives 66.7% contradictory, 28.3% unrelated, 0.0% overgeneralised, 5.0% alternative. All four agents scored about 34.2 or less on the bias task.
limits: One illustrative case for method deviation; taxonomy built by authors.
agent_relevance: Mistakes come from skipping the control, so G3 (test on something the answer was not fitted to) should include 'did a baseline run?'.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench - contamination analysis
finding: Tasks were split by difficulty and knowledge cutoff. After controlling for difficulty there is no systematic advantage on pre-cutoff tasks, so the authors see no strong memorisation signal. They state it does not prove its absence.
numbers: Hard-task pairs reported: 15.4 and 24.8; 22.6 and 31.0. Medium: o4-mini 31.9 to 33.6; gpt-5 44.5 to 23.1. Easy: o4-mini 58.9 to 42.1. Difficulty rubric: 3 axes scored 1-3, sum 3-4 Easy, 5-6 Medium, 7-9 Hard.
limits: Cutoff dates approximate; training mix unknown; small groups; arrow direction in extracted text not verified against the figure.
agent_relevance: Historical cases may be in the model's training data. When we use a known case as evidence, treat a good answer as possibly recall, not reasoning.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: rediscovering unseen chemistry hypotheses
finding: Decomposes hypothesis discovery into retrieving inspirations, composing hypotheses, and ranking. Test set of 51 chemistry papers published after January 2024, annotated by PhD chemists with background, inspirations and hypothesis, using a model with a pre-2024 cutoff to avoid contamination.
limits: Matching judged by GPT-4o against experts on a subset; 51 papers; only chemistry; hit ratio means ground-truth inspiration selected, not that a hypothesis is true.
agent_relevance: Post-cutoff cases are a clean way to test a method on cases the model cannot have memorised.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: scientific equation discovery
finding: Known equations (Feynman set) are likely memorised, so the authors rewrite them in less common forms (LSR-Transform) and add synthetic problems (LSR-Synth). Even the best system reaches only 31.5% symbolic accuracy on Transform and 28.1% on Synth. Error curves on the original Feynman set look like recall, not search.
numbers: 239 problems across four domains; Feynman set has 100 equations; best symbolic accuracy 31.5% (LSR-Transform) and 28.1% (LSR-Synth).
limits: Equations are textbook cases, so the memorisation effect is specific to famous historical results.
agent_relevance: Famous historical cases inflate scores. When the agent is shown a famous case, check with a transformed version before trusting it.

source: Duan et al. (2024) Time travel in LLMs: tracing data contamination
finding: Method that detects benchmark contamination by prompting with dataset and partition names and checking if the model completes held-out instances. Their best method matched human experts for 92% to 100% of cases across seven datasets. GPT-4 was found contaminated with AG News, WNLI and XSum; a near-exact GSM8k training instance was also reproduced.
numbers: Accuracy 92-100% over seven datasets, 14 partitions and two models (GPT-4 and GPT-3.5); GSM8k test with GPT-4.
limits: Needs exact dataset names; detects verbatim recall only, not paraphrased knowledge.
agent_relevance: A way to check whether a historical case we give the agent is already memorised.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning (case-based reasoning memory)
finding: An agent that stores past episodes as cases in memory and retrieves them with a learned policy, with no weight updates. Case memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 points on out-of-distribution tasks.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3; GAIA test 79.40%; DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 and 80.4 PM.
limits: Abstract-level numbers read; memory design and ablations not checked. Cases here are agent episodes, not historical cases.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that retrieving past cases can help agents. Retrieval is learned; our design should keep selection in code.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent collects experiences from training tasks, extracts natural-language insights and recalls past experiences at inference. Performance rises as experience accumulates.
numbers: No headline figure read in the abstract; see benchmark tables in the paper.
limits: Only the abstract and front matter were read; per-benchmark effects unverified.
agent_relevance: Insights extracted from cases are used as rules; we should test those rules on held-out items before keeping them.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Head-to-head human study: LLM ideas judged more novel than expert ideas (p < 0.05) and slightly weaker on feasibility. LLM self-evaluation failed and generation lacked diversity.
numbers: More than 100 NLP researchers wrote ideas and gave blind reviews.
limits: Judged novelty is not realised outcome; the authors propose an execution study.
agent_relevance: Judging by reviewers and by an LLM both fail as tests of a method claim; outcomes must be executed.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: virtual environment for automated scientific discovery
finding: Environment with 120 challenge tasks in eight topics, three difficulty levels each; strong baseline agents struggle on most tasks.
numbers: 120 tasks; 8 topics; 3 levels; three automatic metrics (task completion, relevant actions, discovered knowledge).
limits: Simulated worlds, so memory of history does not help, but they differ from real history.
agent_relevance: A contamination-free test bed for any case-derived method rule.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: Benchmark formalising multi-step data-driven discovery; tasks derived from published papers. Best system scores only 25%.
numbers: 264 tasks in 6 domains plus 903 synthetic tasks.
limits: Tasks derived by hand from papers; abstract-level numbers.
agent_relevance: Published studies as test cases work, but scores are low, so claims from LLM case use need to be small.

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench: rigorous assessment of language agents for data-driven discovery
finding: 102 tasks drawn from 44 peer-reviewed papers and validated by nine experts. Best agent solves 32.4% alone, 34.3% with expert knowledge, and OpenAI o1-preview reaches 42.2% at more than 10 times the cost.
numbers: 102 tasks; 44 papers; 3 frameworks; 5 LLMs; 3 attempts per task.
limits: Code-generation tasks, not method discovery.
agent_relevance: Expert-provided knowledge adds little (about 1.9 points); extra compute adds more but costs 10 times as much.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Large language models for automated open-domain scientific hypotheses discovery (MOOSE)
finding: First dataset for social-science hypothesis discovery from raw web text, with a multi-module framework and three feedback loops. Reported as the first work showing LLMs can generate novel and valid hypotheses, by GPT-4 and expert evaluation.
numbers: No specific figure retained from the abstract.
limits: Evaluation partly by GPT-4; domain is social science.
agent_relevance: Feedback loops that cite real output match our G2.

source: Large language models for history, philosophy, and sociology of science: interpretive uses and methodological challenges (Studies in HPS Part A, 2026)
finding: A 2026 Studies in HPS Part A paper on LLM use in HPSS appeared in a Crossref search; its content was not retrievable. A related edited-volume chapter, 'Doing science studies with large language models', was also listed.
numbers: Crossref shows 4 citations (Nov 2026).
limits: Authors not confirmed; title and venue only; page blocked at redirect.
agent_relevance: To read next: nearest source on LLMs doing HPS-style case work.

source: Lean et al. (2023) Digital literature analysis for empirical philosophy of science
finding: A BJPS paper proposing digital text analysis as a method for empirical philosophy of science; cited by Herfeld as a programmatic proposal.
numbers: Crossref: 14 citations; no figures read.
limits: Full text not obtained.
agent_relevance: Shows that computational reading of the literature is already proposed as a way to widen case selection.
